reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A rapidly growing mycobacterium closely related to the M. abscessus and M. chelonae group, from which it was formerly indistinguishable without molecular methods
Its best-known niche is metalworking fluid, where contamination has caused outbreaks of hypersensitivity pneumonitis among machine-shop workers
Also found in water systems and contaminated solutions, and a cause of catheter-related and other health-care-associated infection
The occupational lung disease is an immune (hypersensitivity) reaction to aerosolised organisms rather than invasive infection
True infection includes bloodstream infection related to intravascular catheters and skin or soft-tissue infection after procedures
Reliable identification requires molecular methods such as rpoB or hsp65 sequencing to separate it from other rapid growers
Like related rapid growers it is often multidrug-resistant with inducible macrolide resistance, so treatment is susceptibility-guided and combined with source removal
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium immunogenum is an environmental rapidly growing mycobacterium closely allied to the M. abscessus and M. chelonae group. Its characteristic reservoir is metalworking fluid, and inhalation of contaminated aerosols provokes hypersensitivity pneumonitis, an immune-mediated reaction to the organism rather than tissue invasion. Where it causes genuine infection, this usually follows inoculation or intravascular-device contamination, giving catheter-related bloodstream infection or post-procedural skin and soft-tissue disease, with biofilm on devices promoting persistence. Its resistance profile resembles that of related rapid growers, including inducible macrolide resistance, so cure depends on susceptibility-guided therapy and removal of the source or device.
additionalDifferentials: Other rapidly growing mycobacteria (M. abscessus, M. chelonae)
Catheter-related bloodstream infection from conventional organisms
Bacterial or fungal post-procedural soft-tissue infection
Occupational asthma or organic dust toxic syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Molecular identification (rpoB or hsp65 sequencing) to distinguish it from related rapid growers
Drug-susceptibility testing including detection of inducible macrolide resistance
Occupational and exposure history with sampling of metalworking fluid in suspected outbreaks
Chest CT and lung assessment for hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Blood and device cultures in suspected catheter-related infection
redFlags: Clustered respiratory illness in machine-shop workers suggesting a contaminated metalworking-fluid source
Catheter-related bloodstream infection requiring line removal
Health-care-associated clusters pointing to a contaminated solution or device
Progressive infection despite therapy, reflecting drug resistance
reference.prognosis: Occupational hypersensitivity pneumonitis usually improves with removal from the offending exposure. Genuine infection carries the guarded outlook of the related rapid growers, being difficult to eradicate with antimicrobials alone; adequate source control, including device removal, is central to a good outcome.
pitfalls: Misidentifying it as M. abscessus or M. chelonae without molecular testing
Treating hypersensitivity pneumonitis as invasive infection instead of removing the exposure
Relying on a macrolide without testing for inducible resistance
Failing to remove an infected catheter or identify a contaminated solution
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
